PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 45 — Lesson 69: Dermatologic Assessment & Diagnostics

FNP-level goal: Describe skin findings precisely, recognize time-sensitive dermatologic emergencies, distinguish inflammatory, infectious, allergic, drug-related, neoplastic, and systemic patterns, and use photographs, testing, biopsy/referral, and follow-up safely. The goal is not to diagnose every rash by appearance alone; it is to match morphology, distribution, time course, exposures, symptoms, and patient risk to a safe clinical plan.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a standardized vocabulary to describe primary and secondary skin lesions.
  • Build a rash or lesion problem representation using morphology, distribution, symptoms, timing, exposures, and systemic context.
  • Recognize red flags for severe infection, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, severe cutaneous adverse reactions, vasculitic/purpuric illness, and skin cancer.
  • Differentiate common outpatient patterns from presentations that need emergency or expedited dermatology evaluation.
  • Choose targeted tests, cultures, microscopy, biopsy/referral, and photographs to answer a clinical question.
  • Provide inclusive skin assessment and clear safety-net instructions across all skin tones.

Part 1 — Start With Stability, Pain, and Systemic Illness

A skin complaint can be a visible sign of systemic disease. Assess vital signs, mental status, appearance, severe pain, rapid progression, fever, mucosal involvement, eye symptoms, respiratory symptoms, hypotension, immunocompromise, pregnancy, medication exposure, wounds/bites, and recent procedures. Pain out of proportion, rapidly expanding erythema, bullae, skin duskiness/necrosis, crepitus, systemic toxicity, or unstable physiology requires immediate emergency evaluation for serious soft-tissue infection or another high-consequence process.

Do not be reassured by a small visible surface area if the patient is profoundly ill, has severe pain, or has high-risk context such as diabetes, immune suppression, peripheral vascular disease, recent surgery, trauma, injection drug use, or a rapidly progressive course. The diagnosis “cellulitis” should not substitute for assessment of abscess, necrotizing infection, DVT, dermatitis, zoster, ischemia, drug reaction, or other mimics.

Part 2 — Describe Before You Diagnose

Document lesion type, color, border, scale, surface, size, number, configuration, blanching, tenderness, warmth, drainage, and evolution. Primary lesions include macules, papules, plaques, nodules, vesicles, bullae, pustules, wheals, and purpura. Secondary changes include scale, crust, erosion, ulceration, excoriation, fissure, lichenification, atrophy, and scarring. A useful description is specific enough that another clinician can visualize it without seeing the patient.

Map the distribution: localized versus generalized; symmetric versus asymmetric; flexural, extensor, acral, intertriginous, dermatomal, photo-distributed, mucosal, palms/soles, scalp, nails, or genital involvement. Ask whether lesions are pruritic, painful, burning, numb, tender, or asymptomatic. The same morphology means different things in different distributions and patient contexts.

Part 3 — Time Course, Exposure, and Medication History

Ask when the eruption began, how quickly it spread, what appeared first, and whether there were prior episodes. Review new prescriptions, dose changes, OTC products, supplements, vaccines, antibiotics, antiseizure drugs, NSAIDs, allopurinol, biologics, topical agents, and contrast exposure. Ask about household contacts, travel, work/animal exposures, sexual history when relevant, new cosmetics/detergents, plants, sun exposure, bites, trauma, and recent infection.

A medication may be temporally related without being causal, and a familiar medication can still contribute after a dose change or interaction. Conversely, do not label every new rash “drug allergy” without documenting morphology, timing, mucosal/systemic features, and alternative causes. Accurate documentation protects future prescribing and avoids both repeat exposure and unnecessary loss of beneficial therapies.

Part 4 — Inflammatory and Allergic Patterns

Pruritus, eczematous scale, ill-defined patches, contact distribution, and recurrent flares may suggest inflammatory or contact processes, but infection, infestation, drug eruption, and systemic disease remain part of the differential. Urticaria is typically transient and migratory; the key safety question is whether there are signs of anaphylaxis such as airway symptoms, wheeze, hypotension, syncope, or significant gastrointestinal symptoms. Those features require emergency management rather than a routine rash visit.

When considering a topical or systemic anti-inflammatory treatment, inspect for infection, ask about fever/pain/purulence, and consider the body site, duration, skin integrity, age, pregnancy status, and current treatments. Steroids can modify appearance and increase risk when an untreated infection or severe drug reaction is present. Treat the patient’s risk and diagnostic uncertainty—not only the itch score.

Part 5 — Skin and Soft-Tissue Infection

Cellulitis commonly presents with painful, warm, tender, red, swollen skin and may progress. However, bilateral leg redness, chronic edema, pruritus, scale, sharply demarcated dermatitis, or lack of warmth/tenderness may point toward a noninfectious mimic. Examine for portal of entry, ulcer, interdigital maceration, abscess, fluctuance, lymphangitic streaking, joint involvement, and distal neurovascular status.

Rapidly spreading redness, fever/chills, systemic illness, severe pain, bullae, necrosis, or failure to improve needs urgent reassessment. An abscess may need drainage rather than antibiotics alone; a wound may require culture or procedural care in the appropriate setting. Do not delay emergency transfer when necrotizing infection or sepsis is plausible.

Part 6 — Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

New rash plus fever, facial edema, skin pain, blistering, peeling/detachment, targetoid or dusky lesions, oral/genital/ocular mucosal disease, sore eyes, painful swallowing, respiratory symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, kidney injury, or eosinophilia can signal a severe cutaneous adverse reaction. Suspect a high-risk drug exposure when the timing fits, but assess broadly for infectious and autoimmune causes as well.

Possible Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, or other severe drug reaction requires emergency evaluation and coordinated medication review. Do not manage painful widespread rash with mucosal involvement by simply adding an antihistamine or a routine topical prescription. Document all suspected agents and escalate according to local emergency and specialty pathways.

Part 7 — Purpura, Petechiae, and Nonblanching Lesions

Determine whether red-purple lesions blanch with pressure. Nonblanching petechiae or purpura can reflect platelet/coagulation disorders, vasculitis, infection, embolic disease, medication effects, trauma, or other systemic pathology. Ask about fever, headache/neck stiffness, toxicity, bleeding/bruising, renal symptoms, abdominal pain, arthralgias, anticoagulants, recent infection, and new medications.

Rapidly progressive nonblanching rash with systemic illness, meningismus, hypotension, altered mental status, or bleeding requires emergency evaluation. A stable localized bruise has a different differential from new widespread purpura; morphology never replaces physiologic assessment and a complete review of systems.

Part 8 — Pigmented Lesions and Skin Cancer Safety

For a changing or atypical pigmented lesion, ask about new onset, evolution, bleeding, itching, ulceration, growth rate, personal/family history, prior melanoma/nonmelanoma skin cancer, immune suppression, UV exposure, and prior photographs. The ABCDE framework—Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter, and Evolving—helps identify lesions needing further evaluation. “Evolving” and an “ugly duckling” lesion that differs from a patient’s other nevi are particularly useful prompts, but no checklist rules melanoma in or out.

Examine all relevant sites respectfully, including scalp, nails, palms, soles, mucosa, and intertriginous areas when indicated. Skin cancer can appear on any skin tone and in less sun-exposed locations. A new or changing lesion, nonhealing sore, recurrent bleeding lesion, or suspicious nail pigment requires timely dermatology/biopsy pathway rather than reassurance from a single benign-sounding feature.

Part 9 — Wounds, Ulcers, and Pressure Injury

For an ulcer or wound, document location, dimensions, depth when safely assessable, tissue type, drainage/odor, surrounding erythema, pain, undermining, exposed structures, perfusion, sensation, edema, footwear/pressure, trauma, diabetes control, smoking, nutrition, and vascular history. Do not debride or probe beyond training and protocol. A “diabetic ulcer” is not automatically a superficial skin problem; assess infection, ischemia, neuropathy, bone involvement, and off-loading needs.

Urgent referral or emergency evaluation is needed for spreading infection, systemic illness, ischemic color/coolness, rapidly progressive tissue loss, suspected deep infection, exposed bone/tendon, severe pain with poor perfusion, or inability to manage safe wound care. Coordinate wound care, vascular, podiatry, surgical, infectious-disease, or dermatology involvement according to the clinical question and local pathway.

Part 10 — Tests, Photographs, Biopsy, and Referral

Use tests to answer a question. KOH microscopy, bacterial or viral testing, fungal culture, wound culture, CBC/chemistries, inflammatory studies, pregnancy testing, STI testing, or biopsy may be appropriate depending on morphology and differential. Superficial wound swabs can mislead when the key question is deep infection; a normal basic lab result does not rule out a dangerous skin or systemic process.

With consent and policy-compliant secure tools, serial photographs with scale/location can document change and improve consultation. Protect privacy: do not use personal devices or place identifiable intimate-area images in unapproved channels. Refer urgently for suspected melanoma, nonhealing/bleeding lesions, difficult diagnostic uncertainty, extensive disease, recurrent treatment failure, or a high-risk medication reaction. The FNP responsibility is timely recognition, appropriate workup, treatment within scope, and closed-loop follow-up.

Part 11 — Inclusive Assessment Across Skin Tones

Redness and inflammation may appear as violaceous, brown, gray, deepened, or subtle color change rather than bright erythema in darker skin. Compare to unaffected skin and rely on warmth, swelling, tenderness, texture, pain, drainage, and patient-reported change—not color alone. Avoid using a single textbook image as the reference standard; morphology, distribution, and systemic findings are more reliable when assessed across diverse skin tones.

Ask patients what their skin usually looks like, what changed first, and whether they have photographs from earlier in the course. This improves diagnostic accuracy and respects the patient as a key historian.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Rapidly Progressive Leg Redness

A 56-year-old with diabetes has rapidly enlarging painful lower-leg redness, fever, chills, and new confusion. The area has a bullous region and pain is severe.

FNP reasoning: this is not a routine outpatient “rash.” Rapid progression, systemic toxicity, bullae, and severe pain raise concern for serious soft-tissue infection and sepsis. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation rather than delaying for a routine culture or oral-treatment trial.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: New Medication, Painful Rash, Mucosal Disease

A 27-year-old began a new antiseizure medication two weeks ago and now has fever, painful widespread rash, red eyes, and mouth erosions.

FNP reasoning: fever, skin pain, mucosal involvement, ocular symptoms, and recent medication exposure are severe-reaction red flags. Emergency assessment and coordinated medication review are required; this is not uncomplicated urticaria.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: The Changing Lesion

A 48-year-old reports a dark lesion on the sole that has enlarged and changed color over several months. It occasionally bleeds after being rubbed by a shoe.

FNP reasoning: changing pigmented lesion plus bleeding and acral location requires timely dermatology/biopsy evaluation. Do not dismiss it as trauma or a wart without an appropriate lesion assessment and referral plan.

FNP Dermatology-Assessment Framework

  1. Assess stability first: systemic toxicity, severe pain, rapid progression, mucosal/ocular disease, airway symptoms, and hemodynamics.
  2. Describe accurately: morphology, color, border, scale, blanching, distribution, symptoms, and change over time.
  3. Take a targeted exposure history: medication, infection/contact, travel, sexual, occupational, environmental, wound, and immune-risk context.
  4. Screen for emergencies: necrotizing infection, sepsis, anaphylaxis, severe drug reaction, purpura with systemic illness, and ischemic/deep wound concern.
  5. Consider cancer safety: ABCDE/Evolving, ugly duckling, nonhealing/bleeding lesions, and acral/nail/mucosal sites.
  6. Test with a question: microscopy, culture, labs, photography, biopsy, or specialty referral based on the differential.
  7. Close the loop: documented plan, images only through approved systems, result ownership, specific precautions, and interval reassessment.

High-Yield Summary

Rash evaluation: describe before diagnosing—morphology, distribution, symptoms, timing, exposures, and systemic context.
Cellulitis: rapidly expanding painful red/warm swelling with fever/chills or systemic illness needs urgent reassessment; consider mimics and abscess/deep infection.
Severe drug reaction: fever, painful rash, mucosal/ocular involvement, blistering, or skin detachment requires emergency evaluation.
Purpura: nonblanching lesions plus systemic illness can be an emergency.
Skin cancer: use ABCDE and evolving/ugly-duckling concepts, but refer suspicious changing, bleeding, nonhealing, acral, nail, or mucosal lesions appropriately.
All skin tones: assess warmth, tenderness, texture, swelling, and patient-reported change; erythema may not appear bright red.
FNP standard: combine morphology, risk, systemic assessment, testing purpose, secure documentation, referral, and explicit return precautions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Dermatologic assessment, medication management, cultures/biopsy, wound care, emergency disposition, referral, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
